title: [Newspoint] Drifting away

blocks.text: It does manage to put live, talking people on the stand. But have they got something, anything, to disprove, or at least cast a doubt on, the impeachment charge that Vice President Sara Duterte has unexplained wealth?
The defense has a fundamental problem: it has no witnesses. And that possibly is the reason it is drifting away.

Not even those among them who keep, or have access to, documents and records that may be of help to Duterte admit, on cross examination, that they have not so much as laid eyes on any such exculpatory evidence. No wonder their testimonies go around and around. But trust pro-Duterte senator-judges to exploit the situation by way of an “intervention” — that’s the privilege senator-judges have of inserting themselves at just about any time during the hearings to put questions to the witness on the stand or parties to the trial or simply to speak their minds as they please.

The last hearing before the impeachment court took a break last week for the ASEAN meeting had provided an occasion for one of the more obvious and strained of those interventions. On the stand was a friend of Manases Carpio’s. Carpio figures at the trial being Sara Duterte’s husband, as co-owner with her of whatever wealth credited to her, explained or unexplained, and vice versa.

I’m still trying to explain to myself how a one-time, quarter-of-a-million-peso personal expense by Carpio on sneakers to give away could be fair subject of testimony. Well, I can only guess that it is to do with the singular nature of the trial, one conducted not by professional judges but by senators, making it as much a political as a judicial process.

In any case, the defense promoted Carpio’s gesture as a virtue. The prosecution, on the other hand, attacked it from the perspective of the constitutional provision admonishing public officials and their families to live simple lifestyles, an admonishment that ought to vibrate with singular resonance in a lopsided society like ours.

Senator-judge Pia Cayetano herself sounded incredulous and expressed herself with the passion she is known to bring to any public role she takes on, although this time, sans tears. Actually, her impassioned yet dry performance rather suited the preachy point she was making: How could anyone — like me — have missed Manases Carpio’s great benefaction!

The problem was this: Not only was the size of the largesse scandalous, the bestowal seemed misplaced — it didn’t really benefit the truly needy, let alone the desperate poor, thus constituting such precise ostentatious display of wealth as the Constitution disallows and also making Carpio’s friend Chadrin Parian witness to patronage, in fact a beneficiary of it, by his own admission.

If anything, Pia Cayetano has been consistent through the trial — consistent, that is, in her support for the impeached. To be sure, she has her counterparts on the court, not surprising, really, in proceedings where politicking cannot be avoided, as precisely the case with an impeachment trial.

Cayetano’s politicking can be a trifle too tawdry, though. In defense of Carpio, she did not stop at extolling his patronage; she even gave two popular and current examples for good measure. But then, again, the problem was that one was a false example, and the other even tended to show precisely how patronage could trump a potentially fair and virtuous arrangement.

Our own Alex Eala, the world-tennis phenomenon, owed no patron, hadn’t needed one. She got to where she is much on her own — her own talent, her own determination, her own initiative, her own hard work, her own sweat and tears. On the other hand, pole-vaulter EJ Obiena seems to me just the type to find use for a patron like Carpio.

Obiena was a state-accredited athlete. That assured him the money and other things he needed to fulfill his promise. Just as he began to rise to world class, the Philippine Sports Commission, the agency in charge of him, suspected him of fund misuse and suspended his entitlements. But before he could clear himself, the Philippine Olympic Committee, a nongovernmental organization running on private sponsorships and subsidies, took over as his patron — not unlike an institutional Manases Carpio.

In a further attempt to show that nothing was wrong with Carpio’s quarter-of-a-million-peso gesture, Cayetano cited her own family’s generosity toward athletes. While I’m prepared to give her and her family the benefit of the doubt, I find the circumstances in Carpio’s case simply too scandalous for him to deserve any excuses.

All that said, I realize that the trial has been going off-course and that I, for one, have allowed myself to be carried along. My own excuse is that I just cannot leave alone anything thrown in the air for all to hear that needs straightening out. It’s a professional compulsion. – Rappler.com
